title: Choose generic type parameters and constraints without replacing type safety with object casts

questions.prompt:
An `IDescribable` interface declares `string Describe()`. A helper receives an existing value, calls `Describe()`, and returns that value with its original static type. Unrelated classes and structs should be supported.

Explain why `T DescribeAndReturn<T>(T value) where T : IDescribable` fits this contract. Why would accepting and returning `object` with an internal cast weaken it, and why are `class`, a shared base class, and `new()` unnecessary constraints?

rubric.point: Explains that the interface constraint guarantees Describe() is available to the generic implementation.
Explains that using T for both parameter and return type preserves the caller's concrete static type.
Explains that the generic constraint rejects unsupported type arguments at compile time, whereas an object-to-interface cast can fail at runtime.
Explains that class excludes structs, a base-class constraint imposes an unnecessary hierarchy, and new() is unnecessary because the value already exists.

questions.model:
`where T : IDescribable` guarantees that the implementation can call `Describe()` without a cast. Using the same `T` for the input and return type preserves the caller's concrete static type.

An `object` parameter accepts values that do not implement `IDescribable`, so an internal cast can fail at runtime. Returning `object` also loses the specific return type and requires the caller to recover it. The generic constraint checks the required capability at compile time.

`class` would exclude supported structs. A shared base class would impose an inheritance relationship the operation does not need. `new()` would require a public parameterless constructor even though the helper receives an existing value and constructs nothing.

questions.prompt:
A conversion helper invokes a supplied function and returns its result. It must support converting a `SensorReading` into a `string`.

Compare these signatures:

- `T Convert<T>(T input, Func<T, T> convert)`
- `TResult Convert<TSource, TResult>(TSource input, Func<TSource, TResult> convert)`

Explain why the second signature expresses the required type relationships better. Does its implementation need constraints on either type parameter if it only invokes `convert(input)`? Explain.

rubric.point: Explains that the first signature uses one type parameter for both input and output, so it cannot express SensorReading and string as distinct static types without widening the contract.
Explains that the second signature allows distinct source and result types while requiring the function to accept TSource and produce TResult, preserving compile-time checks without object casts.
Explains that no constraints are needed because invoking the typed function requires no additional capabilities from TSource or TResult.

questions.model:
The first signature ties the input and output to the same `T`. It cannot directly preserve `SensorReading` as the input type and `string` as the result type. Choosing `object` to accommodate both would lose that precise relationship.

The second signature represents those types independently: `TSource` can be `SensorReading` and `TResult` can be `string`. The delegate connects them by accepting the source type and returning the result type. The compiler checks this relationship, and callers receive a `string` without casting.

Neither type parameter needs a constraint. The helper only invokes the supplied delegate; it does not construct either type or call members on their values.
